subject: Every item has identical DIF statistics in bifactor model

messages.author: c1aa206e366e8133
messages.subject: Every item has identical DIF statistics in bifactor model
parts:
Hi Phil and group,

First off, I'd like to give a huge thanks to you Phil for developing this package and supporting the community here; it has been invaluable as I learn this subject area. This question is for you or anyone else here who may be able to help.

I have a dataframe of 5000 cases, first 20 rows are binary data representing correct responding. row 21 is gender variable as a factor. I'm trying to run DIF analysis with the following code:

dimensions <- c(rep(1,5), rep(2,5), rep(3,10))

#pick one anchor item from each dimension
anchor_items <- colnames(sampledf[,c(2,7,18)])

#perform multigroup analysis
multigroup_Fr <- bfactor(sampledf[,1:20], model = dimensions, group = sampledf$Gender, guess = .25, invariance= c("free_means", "free_var", anchor_items),
SE=TRUE)

difresultsfr <- DIF(MGmodel = multigroup_Fr, which.par = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "d"),
scheme = "drop", items2test = c(1,6,11),p.adjust = 'BH')

I tested just 3 items for this example and the results have each item with identical dif statistics like below:

     

I must be doing something wrong but haven’t been able to pinpoint it. Any help would be very appreciated.

Thanks,

Joe

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Every item has identical DIF statistics in bifactor model
parts:
Hi Joe,

There's a strong to good chance that bifactor models don't work super well with DIF, largely because of their identification constraints to perform the numerical integration efficiently. I don't prevent such inputs, but just want to warn you that care must be taken with these models as they are slightly more constrained at the outset than one might prefer....

Anyway, in this particular case I don't think you want the 'drop' scheme, but rather the 'add' one. Drop is used when you have equality constraints set up across groups but want them removed to see if the model improves; 'add' is the converse, where the item's respective parameters are freely estimated across the groups but you now want to impose an equality constraint to see if the model gets worse. So, drop is looking to see if the model significantly improves (i.e., item has DIF), while add is looking to see if the model gets worse under the constraint (i.e., contains DIF...). A little confusing in the terminology, but both are sides of the same coin. HTH.

Phil

Thanks very much for this advice. Items still had the same DIF estimates though, so based on that and your caution about DIF with bifactor, I decided to just do unidimensional DIF analysis for that part of the project. I really appreciate your help though.

Joe
